h1: Why your IPA loses hop aroma and how an outside review finds it
title: Why Your IPA Loses Hop Aroma | Craft Beer School
desc: Why IPAs lose hop aroma between tank and glass and how an outside review traces the loss: hop storage, dry hopping, oxygen, temperature and age.
teaser: Bright and juicy in the tank, flat and tired in the glass. The aroma went somewhere. It left clues.
standfirst: Hop aroma is the most fragile thing a brewery makes. When an IPA tastes great in the cellar and dull at the bar, the loss happened at a specific step. Finding that step is a matter of sampling in order, not changing hop varieties.
sections:
Brewers whose IPA disappoints often reach for a new hop variety or a bigger dry hop. Sometimes that helps. More often the beer was fine in the tank and lost its aroma somewhere between there and the customer. More hops only means more expensive aroma lost at the same step.

The aroma compounds that make an IPA smell of citrus, tropical fruit and pine are volatile and easily oxidised. They escape with CO2, stick to yeast and filter media, react with oxygen and fade faster in warm storage. Each of those is a stage you can sample.

Hops lose aroma and bitterness from the day they are harvested, faster when warm and exposed to air. Ask how hops are stored. They should sit cold, ideally frozen, in sealed, oxygen-free packs. Opened packs should be flushed, resealed and used quickly. A cold room that doubles as a beer store and gets opened every hour is not good hop storage.

Rub and smell pellets from the current stock against a fresh pack. Grassy, cheesy or flat aroma means the hops were tired before they reached the kettle. Our guide to hop storage and freshness covers the details, which matter a great deal when imported hops spend weeks in transit to India.

How and when dry hops go in changes how much aroma survives. Opening a tank and tipping in pellets lets oxygen in. Adding them during vigorous fermentation lets escaping CO2 carry aroma away, although it also helps scrub oxygen. Contact time, temperature and how the hops are roused all matter. Very long contact can add grassy or vegetal character without more fruit.

Dry hopping also carries a risk known as hop creep: enzymes in the hops break down dextrins, the yeast ferments again, gravity drops and diacetyl can appear. A beer packaged before that settles may over-carbonate and taste buttery.

Check the hop store itself with a thermometer and a logger. A freezer that should be at minus 18 °C but sits several degrees warmer because the door seal is worn will slowly flatten every pack inside it.

Oxygen picked up during transfer, filtration, kegging or canning is the most common cause of fast aroma loss. Hop-forward beers show it first. The aroma fades within days, then a sweet, honey or cardboard note arrives. Our guide to oxidised beer describes how it develops.

An outside review measures dissolved oxygen at each stage: in the tank, after transfer, in the bright tank and in the finished keg or can. In consulting work we often see the cellar doing everything right and a single unpurged hose at packaging undoing it.

Even a well-packaged IPA fades quickly when warm. A keg that sits in a hot store for a week or cans that ride in an unrefrigerated truck lose aroma faster than any brewing mistake. In Indian conditions the cold chain is very often the biggest single factor.

Then there is age. A tap line that pours an IPA for five weeks because it sells slowly will serve tired beer at the end, however well it was made. Matching batch size to how fast the beer sells is part of keeping it fresh.

At the bar, check how long each keg of IPA takes to empty and at what temperature it is stored before it goes on tap. Kegs stacked in a warm back room waiting for a free tap lose aroma before anyone pours them. Ask whether the cold room holds temperature through a busy weekend with the door opening constantly. A cheap temperature logger left in the cold room for a week often settles the argument.
What an outside review looks at

• Hop storage temperature, packaging and the age of stock in use.
  • The dry hop method, timing, temperature and contact time.
  • Dissolved oxygen at each transfer and in the finished package.
  • Storage temperature from brewery to bar.
  • Side-by-side tasting of tank, keg, can and tap samples of the same batch.

The side-by-side tasting is often the moment the answer becomes obvious. If the tank sample is bright and the keg sample is already flat, the loss is at packaging. If keg and can are fine but the tap is tired, the problem is in the bar.
faqs: Will adding more dry hops fix fading aroma?
Usually not on its own. If aroma is being lost to oxygen or warm storage, extra hops only mean more expensive aroma lost at the same step. Find the stage first.
How fast does IPA lose its hop aroma?
It depends heavily on oxygen and temperature. Cold, well-packaged IPA holds up for weeks. Warm storage or high oxygen can flatten it within days.
Enzymes in dry hops break down dextrins so the yeast ferments again. Gravity falls, carbonation rises and diacetyl can appear if the beer is packaged too soon.
